name: Aspirin
route_note: oral tablets (plain, buffered, enteric-coated); IV lysine acetylsalicylate in some countries; suppositories

discovery.note: Acetylation of salicylic acid, itself derived from willow bark salicin; Charles Gerhardt had first made the compound in 1853.

tagline: The original wonder drug: analgesic, antipyretic and lifelong antiplatelet
summary: Aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid, a salicylate that irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase. At analgesic doses it treats pain, fever and inflammation; at low daily doses it is a cornerstone antiplatelet drug for secondary prevention of heart attack and stroke.
mechanism: Aspirin transfers its acetyl group to a serine residue (Ser529/530) in the active site of cyclooxygenase-1 and, less potently, cyclooxygenase-2, permanently blocking the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandin H2.

Platelets lack a nucleus and cannot make new enzyme, so a single low dose suppresses thromboxane A2 production for the platelet's 7–10 day life span. This reduces platelet activation and aggregation, the basis of its use in cardiovascular prevention.
At higher doses, reduced prostaglandin synthesis in tissues and the hypothalamus produces analgesic, anti-inflammatory and antipyretic effects.
uses: Secondary prevention of myocardial infarction and ischaemic stroke
Acute coronary syndrome and after coronary stenting (with a P2Y12 inhibitor)
Pre-eclampsia prevention in high-risk pregnancy (low dose)

history.title: First synthesis
history.detail: Charles Frédéric Gerhardt prepares acetylsalicylic acid in impure form.

history.title: Bayer synthesis
history.detail: Felix Hoffmann at Bayer makes a pure, stable form of acetylsalicylic acid.

history.title: Aspirin launched
history.detail: Bayer registers the 'Aspirin' trademark and markets the drug as a powder, later as tablets.

history.title: Trademark lost
history.detail: Under the Treaty of Versailles Bayer loses the Aspirin trademark in several countries, where 'aspirin' becomes a generic name.

history.title: Mechanism discovered
history.detail: John Vane shows that aspirin-like drugs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis; he shares the 1982 Nobel Prize.

history.title: ISIS-2
history.detail: The ISIS-2 trial shows aspirin reduces vascular mortality after acute myocardial infarction.

history.title: Primary prevention trials
history.detail: ASPREE, ARRIVE and ASCEND find little net benefit of aspirin for primary prevention, with more bleeding.

history.title: USPSTF update
history.detail: The US Preventive Services Task Force recommends against starting low-dose aspirin for primary prevention in adults aged 60 or older.

pk.half_life: ~15–20 min (aspirin); salicylate 2–3 h at low doses, longer at high doses (saturable)
pk.metabolism: Hydrolysed by esterases to salicylate; hepatic conjugation

serious: Reye's syndrome in children and teenagers

facts: The name combines 'a' (acetyl) with 'spir' from Spiraea, the meadowsweet plant that is a source of salicylates.
Its antiplatelet effect is irreversible, lasting for the life of the platelet.
Aspirin is one of the most widely used medicines in the world.

references.title: Vane JR. Inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis as a mechanism of action for aspirin-like drugs. Nature New Biol 1971
